\section[īrāscor, īrāscī]{īrāscor, īrāscī — to grow angry, be angry}

\label{lesson:LA-C493-irascor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for gentle, then the Latin for to soothe.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: īrāscor, īrāscī}
\textbf{īrāscor, īrāscī} — \textquotedblleft{}to grow angry, be angry\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dominus servō īrāscitur, quod cēnam nōn parāvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The master grows angry with the slave because he has not prepared dinner.}
\end{quote}

Deponent: \emph{īrāscor, īrāscī, īrātus sum}, with the dative of the person. \emph{Īrātus}, already known, is its participle.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{īrāscor} is built on \emph{īra} \textquotedblleft{}anger\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-scor}, an ending for a state that begins (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{irascible} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{īrāscor, īrāscī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{īrāscor, īrāscī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{īrāscor, īrāscī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for gentle, then the Latin for to soothe, then say \emph{īrāscor, īrāscī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does īrāscor, īrāscī mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To grow angry, be angry\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum]{īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum — hot-tempered, quick to anger}

\label{lesson:LA-C493-iracundus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to soothe, then the Latin for to grow angry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum}
\textbf{īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum} — \textquotedblleft{}hot-tempered, quick to anger\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Senex īrācundus semper clāmat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The hot-tempered old man is always shouting.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{īra} — anger. A trait of character, where \emph{īrātus} is a passing mood.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{īrācundus} is built on \emph{īra} \textquotedblleft{}anger\textquotedblright{} with the adjective ending \emph{-cundus}, as in \emph{verēcundus} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to soothe, then the Latin for to grow angry, then say \emph{īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum} again
\end{itemize}

\section[īrācundia, īrācundiae]{īrācundia, īrācundiae — a hot temper, irritability}

\label{lesson:LA-C493-iracundia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to grow angry, then the Latin for hot-tempered.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: īrācundia, īrācundiae}
\textbf{īrācundia, īrācundiae} — \textquotedblleft{}a hot temper, irritability\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Īrācundia eius omnēs amīcōs terret.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{His hot temper frightens all his friends.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, first declension, from \emph{īrācundus}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{īrācundia} is built on \emph{īrācundus} \textquotedblleft{}hot-tempered\textquotedblright{}, itself from \emph{īra} \textquotedblleft{}anger\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to grow angry, then the Latin for hot-tempered, then say \emph{īrācundia, īrācundiae} again

\section[indignus, indigna, indignum]{indignus, indigna, indignum — unworthy, undeserving; shameful}

\label{lesson:LA-C493-indignus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for hot-tempered, then the Latin for a hot temper.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: indignus, indigna, indignum}
\textbf{indignus, indigna, indignum} — \textquotedblleft{}unworthy, undeserving; shameful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hoc verbum tē indignum est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This word is unworthy of you.}
\end{quote}

With the ablative: \emph{indignus honōre} — unworthy of honour. The opposite of \emph{dignus}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{indignus} is built on \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{dignus} \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB traces \emph{dignus} to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to take, accept\textquotedblright{}). English \emph{indignity} comes from its noun \emph{indignitās}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{indignus, indigna, indignum}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{indignus, indigna, indignum}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{indignus, indigna, indignum}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for hot-tempered, then the Latin for a hot temper, then say \emph{indignus, indigna, indignum} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does indignus, indigna, indignum mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Unworthy, undeserving; shameful\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[indignor, indignārī]{indignor, indignārī — to be indignant, resent}

\label{lesson:LA-C493-indignor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a hot temper, then the Latin for unworthy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: indignor, indignārī}
\textbf{indignor, indignārī} — \textquotedblleft{}to be indignant, resent\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Cīvēs indignantur, quod tribūtum magnum est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The citizens are indignant that the tax is large.}
\end{quote}

Deponent: \emph{indignor, indignārī, indignātus sum}. To count a thing unworthy, and be angry at it. English \emph{indignant}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{indignor} is built on \emph{indignus} \textquotedblleft{}unworthy\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{indignant} comes from its present participle.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{indignor, indignārī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{indignor, indignārī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{indignor, indignārī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a hot temper, then the Latin for unworthy, then say \emph{indignor, indignārī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does indignor, indignārī mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To be indignant, resent\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
